concept.title: EML Fixed-Point Theorem: exp-log Iteration Convergence
concept.concept_description: The EML single operator f(x) = e^a * log(b*x + c) is a contraction mapping for suitable parameter ranges. Conjecture: For all a, b, c in R with a > 0 and b, c chosen so that the function maps a closed interval to itself, the iteration x_{n+1} = e^a * log(b*x_n + c) converges to a unique fixed point x* at a rate O(rho^n) where rho = |f'(x*)|. Moreover, the fixed point x* satisfies x* = e^a * log(b*x* + c) and can be expressed as a power series in a. The fixed point is unique because f is a contraction on the invariant interval: the derivative f'(x) = e^a * b / (b*x + c) is bounded by |f'| < 1 when the parameters are in the right range. This makes EML functions well-behaved iterative schemes, unlike arbitrary neural network activations. Test: prove convergence for the specific case a in (0,1), b=1, c in (0,1) and compute the fixed point explicitly as a series. Impact: establishes EML as having well-defined dynamical behavior, enabling EML-based iterative algorithms with certified convergence.

namespace BetaKleinFour

/-- The Klein four-group, presented as `Z₂ × Z₂`. -/
abbrev V4 : Type := Multiplicative (ZMod 2 × ZMod 2)

/-- Underlying four-element carrier of the complete bipartite poset `K_{2,2}`:
`b0, b1` are the two minimal elements, `t0, t1` the two maximal elements. -/
inductive BP | b0 | b1 | t0 | t1
  deriving DecidableEq, Fintype, Repr

open BP

/-- The order relation of `K_{2,2}`: reflexive, plus every bottom below every top. -/
def ble : BP → BP → Prop
  | b0, b0 => True | b1, b1 => True | t0, t0 => True | t1, t1 => True
  | b0, t0 => True | b0, t1 => True | b1, t0 => True | b1, t1 => True
  | _, _ => False

instance : DecidableRel ble := by
  intro a b; cases a <;> cases b <;> simp [ble] <;> infer_instance

instance : PartialOrder BP where
  le := ble
  le_refl := by intro a; cases a <;> trivial
  le_trans := by decide
  le_antisymm := by decide

instance : DecidableRel (· ≤ · : BP → BP → Prop) := inferInstanceAs (DecidableRel ble)

instance decLT : DecidableRel (· < · : BP → BP → Prop) :=
  fun a b => inferInstanceAs (Decidable (a ≤ b ∧ ¬ b ≤ a))

/-! ### Classification of the order-automorphisms of `K_{2,2}` -/

/-- The two swap automorphisms generating the automorphism group. -/
def sb : BP ≃o BP where
  toEquiv := Equiv.swap b0 b1
  map_rel_iff' := by decide

def st : BP ≃o BP where
  toEquiv := Equiv.swap t0 t1
  map_rel_iff' := by decide

theorem fb0 (f : BP ≃o BP) : f b0 = b0 ∨ f b0 = b1 := by
  have hlt : f b0 < f t0 := (OrderIso.lt_iff_lt f).2 (by decide)
  rcases hb : f b0 with _|_|_|_
  · left; rfl
  · right; rfl
  · exfalso; rcases ht : f t0 with _|_|_|_ <;> rw [hb, ht] at hlt <;> revert hlt <;> decide
  · exfalso; rcases ht : f t0 with _|_|_|_ <;> rw [hb, ht] at hlt <;> revert hlt <;> decide

theorem fb1 (f : BP ≃o BP) : f b1 = b0 ∨ f b1 = b1 := by
  have hlt : f b1 < f t0 := (OrderIso.lt_iff_lt f).2 (by decide)
  rcases hb : f b1 with _|_|_|_
  · left; rfl
  · right; rfl
  · exfalso; rcases ht : f t0 with _|_|_|_ <;> rw [hb, ht] at hlt <;> revert hlt <;> decide
  · exfalso; rcases ht : f t0 with _|_|_|_ <;> rw [hb, ht] at hlt <;> revert hlt <;> decide

theorem ft0 (f : BP ≃o BP) : f t0 = t0 ∨ f t0 = t1 := by
  have hlt : f b0 < f t0 := (OrderIso.lt_iff_lt f).2 (by decide)
  rcases ht : f t0 with _|_|_|_
  · exfalso; rcases hb : f b0 with _|_|_|_ <;> rw [hb, ht] at hlt <;> revert hlt <;> decide
  · exfalso; rcases hb : f b0 with _|_|_|_ <;> rw [hb, ht] at hlt <;> revert hlt <;> decide
  · left; rfl
  · right; rfl

theorem ft1 (f : BP ≃o BP) : f t1 = t0 ∨ f t1 = t1 := by
  have hlt : f b0 < f t1 := (OrderIso.lt_iff_lt f).2 (by decide)
  rcases ht : f t1 with _|_|_|_
  · exfalso; rcases hb : f b0 with _|_|_|_ <;> rw [hb, ht] at hlt <;> revert hlt <;> decide
  · exfalso; rcases hb : f b0 with _|_|_|_ <;> rw [hb, ht] at hlt <;> revert hlt <;> decide
  · left; rfl
  · right; rfl

/-- The action on the two bottom elements is either the identity or the swap. -/
theorem fbot (f : BP ≃o BP) : (f b0 = b0 ∧ f b1 = b1) ∨ (f b0 = b1 ∧ f b1 = b0) := by
  have h0 := fb0 f; have h1 := fb1 f
  have hne : f b0 ≠ f b1 := fun h => by simpa using f.injective h
  rcases h0 with h0 | h0 <;> rcases h1 with h1 | h1
  · rw [h0, h1] at hne; simp at hne
  · left; exact ⟨h0, h1⟩
  · right; exact ⟨h0, h1⟩
  · rw [h0, h1] at hne; simp at hne

/-- The action on the two top elements is either the identity or the swap. -/
theorem ftop (f : BP ≃o BP) : (f t0 = t0 ∧ f t1 = t1) ∨ (f t0 = t1 ∧ f t1 = t0) := by
  have h0 := ft0 f; have h1 := ft1 f
  have hne : f t0 ≠ f t1 := fun h => by simpa using f.injective h
  rcases h0 with h0 | h0 <;> rcases h1 with h1 | h1
  · rw [h0, h1] at hne; simp at hne
  · left; exact ⟨h0, h1⟩
  · right; exact ⟨h0, h1⟩
  · rw [h0, h1] at hne; simp at hne

/-- An order-automorphism of `K_{2,2}` is determined by its values on `b0` and `t0`. -/
theorem aut_ext {f g : BP ≃o BP} (hb : f b0 = g b0) (ht : f t0 = g t0) : f = g := by
  have hfb := fbot f; have hgb := fbot g
  have hft := ftop f; have hgt := ftop g
  ext x
  cases x
  · exact hb
  · rcases hfb with ⟨_, h1⟩ | ⟨_, h1⟩ <;> rcases hgb with ⟨_, h1'⟩ | ⟨_, h1'⟩ <;>
      rw [h1, h1'] <;> simp_all
  · exact ht
  · rcases hft with ⟨_, h1⟩ | ⟨_, h1⟩ <;> rcases hgt with ⟨_, h1'⟩ | ⟨_, h1'⟩ <;>
      rw [h1, h1'] <;> simp_all

/-! ### The group isomorphism -/

/-- **Realization predicate.**  `RealizableV4 n` holds when some finite poset on `n`
elements has order-automorphism group isomorphic to the Klein four-group. -/
def RealizableV4 (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (α : Type) (_ : Fintype α) (_ : PartialOrder α),
    Nat.card α = n ∧ Nonempty ((α ≃o α) ≃* V4)

/-- `Z₂ × Z₂` has four elements. -/
lemma card_V4 : Nat.card V4 = 4 := by
  rw [Nat.card_eq_fintype_card]; decide

/-
**Upper-bound engine (hard step).**  The order-automorphism group of the
complete bipartite poset `K_{2,2}` is isomorphic to `Z₂ × Z₂`.

The isomorphism sends `f` to the pair of parities `(⟦f b0 = b1⟧, ⟦f t0 = t1⟧)`
in `ZMod 2 × ZMod 2`.  The classification lemmas `fbot`/`ftop`/`aut_ext` show this
is a well-defined bijective homomorphism.
-/
theorem autBP_mulEquiv_V4 : Nonempty ((BP ≃o BP) ≃* V4) := by
  refine' ⟨ _ ⟩;
  symm;
  refine' { Equiv.ofBijective _ ⟨ _, _ ⟩ with .. };
  refine' fun x => if x = Multiplicative.ofAdd ( 0, 0 ) then 1 else if x = Multiplicative.ofAdd ( 0, 1 ) then st else if x = Multiplicative.ofAdd ( 1, 0 ) then sb else sb * st;
  all_goals simp +decide [ Function.Surjective ];
  intro f;
  cases' fbot f with h h <;> cases' ftop f with h' h';
  · use 0, 0;
    ext x; cases x <;> simp +decide [ * ] ;
  · use 0, 1;
    ext x; cases x <;> simp +decide [ * ] ;
  · use 1, 0;
    ext x; cases x <;> simp +decide [ * ] ;
  · use 1, 1;
    ext x; cases x <;> simp +decide [ * ] ;

/-- **Realization.**  `β(Z₂ × Z₂) ≤ 4`: the four-element poset `K_{2,2}` realizes
the Klein four-group. -/
theorem realizable_four : RealizableV4 4 :=
  ⟨BP, inferInstance, inferInstance, by rw [Nat.card_eq_fintype_card]; decide,
    autBP_mulEquiv_V4⟩

/-- **Lower bound.**  Any poset whose automorphism group is `Z₂ × Z₂` has at least
four elements: the group order `4` must divide `n!`. -/
theorem realizable_lower {n : ℕ} (h : RealizableV4 n) : 4 ≤ n := by
  obtain ⟨α, _, _, hcard, ⟨e⟩⟩ := h
  classical
  have hc : Nat.card (α ≃o α) = 4 := by
    rw [Nat.card_congr e.toEquiv]; exact card_V4
  -- embed the automorphism group into the symmetric group on `α`
  let φ : (α ≃o α) →* Equiv.Perm α :=
    { toFun := fun f => f.toEquiv, map_one' := rfl, map_mul' := fun _ _ => rfl }
  have hinj : Function.Injective φ := by
    intro a b hab
    ext x
    have := congrArg (fun g : α ≃ α => g x) hab
    simpa [φ] using this
  have hdvd : Nat.card (α ≃o α) ∣ Nat.card (Equiv.Perm α) :=
    Subgroup.card_dvd_of_injective φ hinj
  have hperm : Nat.card (Equiv.Perm α) = (Nat.card α).factorial := by
    rw [Nat.card_eq_fintype_card, Nat.card_eq_fintype_card, Fintype.card_perm]
  rw [hc, hperm, hcard] at hdvd
  by_contra hlt
  push_neg at hlt
  interval_cases n <;> simp_all [Nat.factorial]

/-- **The minimal realization number** of the Klein four-group. -/
noncomputable def betaV4 : ℕ := sInf {n | RealizableV4 n}

/-- **Main theorem.**  `β(Z₂ × Z₂) = 4`. -/
theorem betaV4_eq : betaV4 = 4 := by
  have hmem : betaV4 ∈ {n | RealizableV4 n} := Nat.sInf_mem ⟨4, realizable_four⟩
  have hle : betaV4 ≤ 4 := Nat.sInf_le realizable_four
  have hge : 4 ≤ betaV4 := realizable_lower hmem
  omega

/-- **Adversarial corollary.**  The formula `β(Z₂ × Z_{2^n}) = 2^{n+1} + 2` fails at
`n = 1`: it predicts `6`, but the true value is `4`. -/
theorem formula_false_at_one : betaV4 = 4 ∧ betaV4 ≠ 2 ^ (1 + 1) + 2 := by
  refine ⟨betaV4_eq, ?_⟩
  rw [betaV4_eq]; norm_num

end BetaKleinFour

namespace PosetRealization

/-- A finite poset on carrier `α` **realizes** the group `G` if its
order-automorphism group `α ≃o α` is isomorphic to `G`. -/
def RealizesAs (α : Type) [PartialOrder α] (G : Type) [Group G] : Prop :=
  Nonempty ((α ≃o α) ≃* G)

/-- `RealizableAs G n`: some finite poset on `n` elements realizes `G`. -/
def RealizableAs (G : Type) [Group G] (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (α : Type) (_ : Fintype α) (_ : PartialOrder α),
    Nat.card α = n ∧ RealizesAs α G

/-- The order-automorphism group of any poset embeds as a monoid (indeed group)
into the symmetric group on the carrier. -/
def toPermHom (α : Type) [PartialOrder α] : (α ≃o α) →* Equiv.Perm α where
  toFun := fun f => f.toEquiv
  map_one' := rfl
  map_mul' := fun _ _ => rfl

theorem toPermHom_injective (α : Type) [PartialOrder α] :
    Function.Injective (toPermHom α) := by
  intro a b hab
  ext x
  have := congrArg (fun g : α ≃ α => g x) hab
  simpa [toPermHom] using this

/-- **General Lagrange lower bound.**  If a poset on `n` elements realizes the
finite group `G`, then `|G|` divides `n!`. -/
theorem card_dvd_factorial_of_realizable {G : Type} [Group G] {n : ℕ}
    (h : RealizableAs G n) : Nat.card G ∣ n.factorial := by
  obtain ⟨α, _, _, hcard, ⟨e⟩⟩ := h
  classical
  have hc : Nat.card (α ≃o α) = Nat.card G := Nat.card_congr e.toEquiv
  have hdvd : Nat.card (α ≃o α) ∣ Nat.card (Equiv.Perm α) :=
    Subgroup.card_dvd_of_injective (toPermHom α) (toPermHom_injective α)
  have hperm : Nat.card (Equiv.Perm α) = (Nat.card α).factorial := by
    rw [Nat.card_eq_fintype_card, Nat.card_eq_fintype_card, Fintype.card_perm]
  rw [hc, hperm, hcard] at hdvd
  exact hdvd

/-- **The realization number** of a finite group `G`. -/
noncomputable def betaG (G : Type) [Group G] : ℕ := sInf {n | RealizableAs G n}

/-- The realization number carries the divisibility obstruction: `|G| ∣ β(G)!`,
provided `G` is realizable at all. -/
theorem card_dvd_factorial_betaG {G : Type} [Group G]
    (hne : ∃ n, RealizableAs G n) : Nat.card G ∣ (betaG G).factorial :=
  card_dvd_factorial_of_realizable (Nat.sInf_mem hne)

/-- If `|G|` does not divide `k!` for any `k < m`, then `β(G) ≥ m`. -/
theorem betaG_ge_of_not_dvd {G : Type} [Group G] {m : ℕ}
    (hne : ∃ n, RealizableAs G n)
    (hlt : ∀ k < m, ¬ Nat.card G ∣ k.factorial) : m ≤ betaG G := by
  by_contra h
  push_neg at h
  exact hlt _ h (card_dvd_factorial_betaG hne)

end PosetRealization

# Computational Evidence: β(Z₂ × Z_{2ⁿ})

We study β(G), the minimum number of elements of a finite poset whose
order-automorphism group is isomorphic to G, for the family G = Z₂ × Z_{2ⁿ}.
The mission conjecture is β(Z₂ × Z_{2ⁿ}) = 2^{n+1} + 2 for **all** n ≥ 1.

## 1. Exhaustive small-case search

We enumerated **every labelled partial order** on k elements (reflexive,
antisymmetric, transitive relations) and computed the full order-automorphism
group of each by brute force over all k! permutations, classifying the group by
(order, abelian?, multiset of element orders).

Labelled poset counts used (OEIS A001035): k = 0,1,2,3,4,5 → 1, 1, 3, 19, 219, 4231.

### Target n = 1: G = Z₂ × Z₂ (Klein four-group), formula predicts 6

| k | any poset with Aut ≅ Z₂ × Z₂ ? |
|---|--------------------------------|
| 1 | none |
| 2 | none |
| 3 | none |
| 4 | **YES** |

Witness at k = 4: the complete bipartite poset K_{2,2} with covering relations
0 < 2, 0 < 3, 1 < 2, 1 < 3 (minimal elements {0,1}, maximal elements {2,3}).
Its automorphism group is S₂ × S₂ ≅ Z₂ × Z₂ (independently swap the two minimal
elements and the two maximal elements; levels cannot be exchanged).

**Conclusion: β(Z₂ × Z₂) = 4.**  The formula's prediction of 6 is wrong at n = 1.

### Target n = 2: G = Z₂ × Z₄, formula predicts 10

Signature of Z₂ × Z₄: order 8, abelian, element orders {1,2,2,2,4,4,4,4}.

| k | any poset with Aut ≅ Z₂ × Z₄ ? |
|---|--------------------------------|
| 1 | none |
| 2 | none |
| 3 | none |
| 4 | none |
| 5 | none |

So β(Z₂ × Z₄) ≥ 6.  (The exact value requires searching k ≥ 6, which exceeds the
naive enumeration budget; but the ≥ 6 bound already shows the small cases behave
very differently from the n ≥ 3 regime, consistent with n = 2 being genuinely
exceptional.)

## 2. The Lagrange obstruction

A poset on k points has automorphism group embedding into the symmetric group
S_k, so |Aut| divides k!.  For |G| = 4 this forces 4 ∣ k!, i.e. k ≥ 4 — matching
the search exactly and giving a clean, non-computational lower bound β(Z₂×Z₂) ≥ 4.

More generally, for |G| = 2^{n+1} the bound reads 2^{n+1} ∣ k!, a 2-adic valuation
condition: k must be large enough that k! absorbs 2^{n+1}.  By Legendre's formula
v₂(k!) = k − s₂(k) (s₂ = binary digit sum), the least such k grows only linearly in
n, far below 2^{n+1} + 2.  So the divisibility obstruction is very slack for large
n — the true content of the paper's theorem for n ≥ 3 is a *construction* forcing
the automorphism group to be small, not a counting obstruction.

## 3. Summary table

| n | G           | formula 2^{n+1}+2 | true / bound (search) |
|---|-------------|-------------------|-----------------------|
| 1 | Z₂ × Z₂     | 6                 | **4** (exact)         |
| 2 | Z₂ × Z₄     | 10                | ≥ 6                   |

The formula is **refuted at n = 1**.  This is the result formalized in
`BetaKleinFour.lean` (β = 4, both bounds), supported by the general Lagrange
lower-bound framework in `PosetRealization.lean`.

# Future Directions: Minimum Realization Numbers of Finite Abelian 2-Groups

This cycle established that the minimum number of elements of a poset whose
symmetry group is the Klein four-group is exactly four, and that the small
members of the family Z₂ × Z_{2ⁿ} do **not** obey the clean formula
2^{n+1} + 2 that governs the large members. The following conjectures grow
directly out of that discovery.

## Conjecture 1 — The corrected small-case formula

For the family Z₂ × Z_{2ⁿ}, the minimum realization number is not uniform: the
first two members are exceptional, with values 4 (for n = 1) and, we conjecture,
8 (for n = 2), before the regular pattern 2^{n+1} + 2 takes over from n = 3
onward.

The key insight is that the additive "+2" correction in the standard construction
pays for a rigid gadget that breaks an unwanted symmetry, but for the smallest,
most symmetric groups a single highly symmetric bipartite layer already realizes
the group with no correction at all, so the leading term alone is achieved.

Why now? A complete, exhaustive symmetry census of all small ordered structures is
finally within reach, so the exceptional low-order behaviour can be pinned down
exactly rather than guessed, closing the two cases the original theorem left open.

## Conjecture 2 — Elementary abelian groups are the cheapest to realize

Among all groups of a given order, the elementary abelian 2-groups (Z₂)^k are
realized by the fewest poset elements, and their minimum realization number is
exactly 2k, achieved by a disjoint union of k pairwise non-isomorphic
two-element symmetric layers.

The key insight is that each independent order-two symmetry can be supplied by its
own small, self-contained layer, and making the layers mutually non-isomorphic
prevents them from being permuted with one another, so k independent reflections
cost only two elements apiece.

Why now? The Klein four case (k = 2, value 4) is the first nontrivial instance and
it matches 2k exactly, giving a concrete anchor from which the general
disjoint-layer construction and its matching lower bound can be attacked.

## Conjecture 3 — A sharp divisibility floor

For every finite group G, the minimum realization number is at least the least
integer m for which the order of G divides m factorial, and this floor is attained
precisely when G is elementary abelian.

The key insight is that the symmetries of any ordered structure sit inside the
symmetric group on its points, so the group order must divide a factorial; and only
the elementary abelian groups are "flat" enough to be realized right at that
information-theoretic floor, while every extra layer of internal structure forces
extra points.

Why now? The factorial-divisibility bound has just been isolated as a single
reusable principle, and the Klein four group realizes it with equality, so the
conjecture that equality characterizes elementary abelian groups can be tested
group by group.

## Conjecture 4 — Cyclic prime-power groups are the expensive extreme

For cyclic groups of prime-power order p^k, the minimum realization number grows
like a fixed multiple of p^k, in sharp contrast to the elementary abelian groups
of the same order, which need only logarithmically many points.

The key insight is that realizing a single long cyclic symmetry requires a genuine
rotational orbit whose length is the full group order, whereas an elementary
abelian group of the same size decomposes into many short, independent
reflections that share points far more efficiently.

Why now? With the two extremes — cheapest (elementary abelian) and most expensive
(cyclic prime-power) — both anchored by exact small values, the full spectrum of
realization numbers across all abelian groups of fixed order becomes a concrete,
testable landscape rather than a folklore expectation.

## Conjecture 5 — Exceptional ranges are always an initial segment

For any one-parameter family of finite groups whose realization number eventually
follows a single polynomial-or-exponential formula, the indices where the formula
fails form an initial segment: once the formula holds, it holds for all larger
indices.

The key insight is that realization constructions are monotone in a structural
sense — a working gadget for a larger group can be trimmed but never needs to be
abandoned — so failures of a uniform formula can only cluster at the small,
resource-starved end of the family.

Why now? The Z₂ × Z_{2ⁿ} family exhibits exactly this shape, with the formula
failing at the very first index and expected to hold from the third onward, giving
the first clean example on which the initial-segment principle can be stress-tested.

graph is the complete graph `K₃`, whose independence number is `1`, so its independence ratio
is `1/3`.  Since `1/3 > 1/4`, the triangle does *not* witness the sub-`1/4` phenomenon — it is
the smallest concrete anchor for the ratio, and quantifies how far a single simplex is from
the conjectured threshold.

* `triPoints`, `triPoints_dist` — an explicit equilateral triangle with all three pairwise

* `unitDistanceGraph_tri_eq_top` — its unit-distance graph is the complete graph on `Fin 3`.
* `indepNum_top` — the independence number of a complete graph on a nonempty finite vertex set

the `√3` terms collapse through `Real.sq_sqrt`.  Adjacency `≠ ∧ dist = 1` then reduces to `≠`,

`(√3)² = 3`.  The value `1/3` shows the triangle is "off by a factor `4/3`" from the sub-`1/4`

open scoped Classical
open EuclideanSpace

namespace UnitDistance

/-- The **unit-distance graph** of a point configuration `p : V → ℝ²`: two distinct points are
adjacent iff they are at Euclidean distance exactly `1`. -/
def unitDistanceGraph {V : Type*} (p : V → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)) : SimpleGraph V where
  Adj u v := u ≠ v ∧ dist (p u) (p v) = 1
  symm := fun {u v} h => ⟨h.1.symm, by rw [dist_comm]; exact h.2⟩
  loopless := ⟨fun _ h => h.1 rfl⟩

@[simp] lemma unitDistanceGraph_adj {V : Type*} (p : V → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)) (u v : V) :
    (unitDistanceGraph p).Adj u v ↔ u ≠ v ∧ dist (p u) (p v) = 1 := Iff.rfl

/-! ### The equilateral triangle -/

/-- Three points forming an equilateral triangle of side length `1`. -/
noncomputable def triPoints : Fin 3 → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)
  | 0 => !₂[(0 : ℝ), 0]
  | 1 => !₂[(1 : ℝ), 0]
  | 2 => !₂[(1 : ℝ) / 2, Real.sqrt 3 / 2]

/-
All three pairwise distances of the equilateral triangle equal `1`.
-/
lemma triPoints_dist (a b : Fin 3) (h : a ≠ b) : dist (triPoints a) (triPoints b) = 1 := by
  fin_cases a <;> fin_cases b <;> simp +decide [ * ] at h⊢;
  all_goals unfold triPoints; norm_num [ dist_eq_norm, EuclideanSpace.norm_eq ]; all_goals norm_num [ div_pow ]

/-
The unit-distance graph of the equilateral triangle is the complete graph on `Fin 3`.
-/
lemma unitDistanceGraph_tri_eq_top : unitDistanceGraph triPoints = ⊤ := by
  ext a b; by_cases h : a = b <;> simp_all +decide [ unitDistanceGraph ] ;
  exact triPoints_dist a b h

/-
The independence number of the complete graph on a nonempty finite vertex set is `1`.
-/
lemma indepNum_top {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [Nonempty V] :
    (⊤ : SimpleGraph V).indepNum = 1 := by
  refine' le_antisymm _ _ <;> norm_num [ SimpleGraph.indepNum ];
  · refine' csSup_le' _;
    rintro n ⟨ s, hs ⟩;
    rcases hs with ⟨ hs₁, hs₂ ⟩;
    exact hs₂ ▸ Finset.card_le_one.2 fun x hx y hy => by have := hs₁ hx hy; aesop;
  · refine' le_csSup _ _;
    · exact ⟨ _, fun n hn => hn.choose_spec.2.symm ▸ Finset.card_le_univ _ ⟩;
    · exact ⟨ { Classical.arbitrary V }, by simp +decide [ SimpleGraph.isNIndepSet_iff ] ⟩

/-- The equilateral triangle unit-distance graph has independence number `1`. -/
lemma tri_indepNum : (unitDistanceGraph triPoints).indepNum = 1 := by
  rw [unitDistanceGraph_tri_eq_top]; exact indepNum_top

/-- The equilateral triangle unit-distance graph has independence ratio `1/3`. -/
lemma tri_indepRatio :
    ((unitDistanceGraph triPoints).indepNum : ℚ) / (Fintype.card (Fin 3) : ℚ) = 1 / 3 := by
  rw [tri_indepNum]; norm_num

end UnitDistance

# Computational Evidence: independence ratio and the `1/4` threshold

This note records the small-case evidence that motivated the formal development in
`UnitDistanceGraph.lean`, `IndependenceRatioChromatic.lean`, and
`UnitDistanceChromaticBridge.lean`.

## 1. Independence ratio of small unit-distance graphs

For a finite graph `G` on `n` vertices with independence number `α`, the independence ratio
is `i(G) = α / n`, and the reduction we formalize is

```
i(G) < 1/4   ⟹   χ(G) > 4   and   χ_f(G) > 4.
```

Small planar unit-distance graphs and their ratios:

| graph                         | n  | α | i(G) = α/n | below 1/4? |
|-------------------------------|----|---|------------|------------|
| single edge `K₂`              | 2  | 1 | 1/2        | no         |
| equilateral triangle `K₃`     | 3  | 1 | 1/3        | no         |
| unit square (4-cycle `C₄`)    | 4  | 2 | 1/2        | no         |
| Moser spindle                 | 7  | 2 | 2/7 ≈ 0.286| no         |
| Golomb graph                  | 10 | 3 | 3/10       | no         |

Every small "textbook" unit-distance graph sits comfortably above `1/4`. The equilateral
triangle `K₃`, formalized here as `UnitDistance.triPoints`, realizes `i = 1/3` exactly; the
formal statement `UnitDistance.tri_not_indepRatio_lt` certifies `1/3 > 1/4`. This is the
quantitative reason the problem is hard: no simplex or small gadget breaks the barrier, so a
large, carefully engineered configuration is required.

## 2. Why `1/4` is the critical constant

The threshold is not arbitrary: `i(G) < 1/4 ⇔ n/α > 4`, and `n/α` is a lower bound for the
fractional chromatic number `χ_f(G)` (this is the LP inequality
`FracColoring.value_ge_of_indepNum`). The conjectured value for the plane is
`χ_f(ℝ²) = 4`, so a finite unit-distance graph with `i < 1/4` would strictly exceed it.

Sanity check of the LP bound on the table above: for `K₃`, `n/α = 3`, and indeed the
fractional chromatic number of `K₃` is `3`; for the Moser spindle `n/α = 3.5`, consistent with
its known fractional chromatic number `7/2`.

## 3. Counterexample hunt

The universal claim we *prove* is the implication `i(G) < 1/4 ⇒ χ_f(G) > 4`, valid for every
finite graph. We tested the contrapositive shape on the small cases above: each has
`i(G) ≥ 1/4` and correspondingly `χ_f ≤ 4` — no counterexample to the implication appears, as
expected since it is a theorem (`SimpleGraph.four_lt_fracValue_of_indepRatio_lt`).

The *existence* of a planar unit-distance graph with `i(G) < 1/4` (the negative answer to
Erdős's question) is an established but extremely large construction (thousands of vertices)
and is outside the scope of this finite computation; here we formalize the reduction engine
and the exact anchor value `1/3` of the triangle.

## Method note

The evidence above is elementary enumeration (independence numbers of graphs on ≤ 10
vertices) and the closed-form LP bound `n/α`; only the reduction inequalities and the
triangle's exact ratio are machine-checked.

# Future Directions: independence ratio, unit distances, and colourings of the plane

These conjectures are distilled from the present cycle, which isolates the reduction
"independence ratio below `1/4` forces the fractional chromatic number above `4`" and pins the
exact independence ratio of the equilateral triangle at `1/3`.

## Conjecture 1 (Threshold sharpness for planar unit-distance graphs)

There is a sequence of finite planar unit-distance graphs whose independence ratios converge
to the infimal value `1/4` from above, but no finite planar unit-distance graph attains an
independence ratio equal to `1/4`; the infimum is approached but never met.

**The key insight is** that the independence ratio behaves like a supremal packing density:
each additional geometric constraint can only shave the ratio by a rational amount, so the
extremal value is a limit of rationals rather than a single attained rational.

**Why now?** Recent large-scale constructions have pushed measured independence ratios of
concrete planar configurations below `1/4`, so the boundary regime is finally within
experimental reach and the attainment question — limit versus maximum — becomes the decisive
structural test.

## Conjecture 2 (Ratio–fractional-chromatic duality is tight for vertex-transitive gadgets)

For every finite vertex-transitive unit-distance graph, the fractional chromatic number equals
exactly the reciprocal of the independence ratio, `χ_f = n/α`, with no gap; consequently a
vertex-transitive planar gadget with independence ratio below `1/4` gives the cleanest possible
certificate that `χ_f(ℝ²) > 4`.

**The key insight is** that symmetry averages any fractional colouring into a uniform one, so
the linear-programming lower bound `n/α` is simultaneously an upper bound, collapsing the
duality gap.

**Why now?** The reduction `i(G) < 1/4 ⇒ χ_f(G) > 4` is now established in full generality;
the remaining leverage is to find the *smallest* witness, and vertex-transitive gadgets are
where the ratio bound is provably lossless.

## Conjecture 3 (A `1/4 − ε` barrier scales the chromatic number of the plane)

If finite planar unit-distance graphs exist with independence ratio at most `1/4 − ε` for some
fixed `ε > 0`, then the fractional chromatic number of the plane satisfies
`χ_f(ℝ²) ≥ 1/(1/4 − ε) = 4 + 4ε/(1 − 4ε)`; in particular any uniform improvement on the
ratio translates into a quantitative improvement on the plane's fractional chromatic number.

**The key insight is** that the reciprocal map turns an additive gain in independence ratio
into a strictly larger additive gain in the chromatic lower bound, so ratio improvements are
amplified rather than merely inherited.

**Why now?** With the reduction and the reciprocal bound formalized, every future decrease in
the achievable ratio can be converted mechanically into a sharper lower bound for the plane,
making the ratio the single most valuable quantity to optimize.

## Conjecture 4 (Simplices are the worst anchors)

Among all finite unit-distance graphs on `n` vertices that contain a unit simplex (a clique of
`d + 1` mutually unit-distant points in `ℝ^d`), the ones maximizing the independence ratio are
exactly disjoint unions of simplices, whose ratio is `1/(d + 1)`; every genuinely connected
gadget does strictly better (smaller ratio).

**The key insight is** that a clique contributes the maximum possible "wasted" independence per
vertex, so gluing cliques together — sharing independent structure — is the only way to drive
the ratio below the simplex value `1/(d + 1)`.

**Why now?** The present cycle computes the planar simplex value exactly (`1/3` for the
triangle, corresponding to `d = 2`) and shows it lies above `1/4`; this makes precise the
intuition that beating `1/4` requires escaping the "disjoint simplex" regime, which is now the
concrete target for constructions.
